How the wind tunnel works

The tunnel computes how light travels through selected spacetime geometries and maps the energy density, expansion, or shift that goes with those geometries.

Run an experiment
Choose a model and change its speed, radius, or wall scale. Turn on Compare two models to use the same launches and field scale in both panels.
Read the views
The 2D slice maps the field across a plane. The 3D view shows the reference-radius surface and photon paths rotated around the symmetry axis. Drag the view or focus it and use the arrow keys. Both comparison panels rotate together.
Compare clocks
The Clock rate map shows proper time per unit of distant lab time for clocks held in place in the model coordinates. Amber marks positions where that motion cannot be followed by a clock.
Save and reproduce
Experiment tools saves runs, exports samples, and tests numerical sensitivity. Guided labs loads examples to explore.
Explore the research
Use Edit equations to try a custom radial profile. Shell experiments shows the separate matter-shell studies. Model equations and sources explains the metrics and links to the papers.

The models are general-relativity experiments. Photon paths and stress–energy maps describe what a prescribed geometry does and what it would require.

Equation editor

Edit a radial function within a metric family. The tunnel recomputes field maps and photon paths from the applied functions.

Expression syntax and assumptions

r is coordinate radius, R is the radius slider, w is wall scale, v is bubble speed (zero for the static shell), and C is compactness. Use pi, explicit multiplication, and + − * / ^ with parentheses. Type - for minus.

Functions: sin, cos, tanh, exp, log, sqrt, abs, min, max, clamp(x, lo, hi), and smooth5(x), a clamped quintic smoothstep.

Use smooth profiles near the region of interest. The editor samples the domain and uses finite differences. Very narrow features can fall between samples. Custom profiles may change the exterior geometry and photon entry behavior.

Model equations and sources

The center clock measures proper time at x = y = z = 0. In the built-in translating bubbles, the shift cancels the bubble motion at the center, giving one second of proper time per second of distant lab time even when the exterior cannot support a comoving clock. The Minkowski control and static matter shell in the main tunnel have unit lapse and stationary clocks run at the lab rate. Shell experiments includes matter-sourced models with a variable lapse and a slower cavity clock.

The simulation prescribes a metric and integrates test photons in its symmetry plane using fourth-order Runge–Kutta. The heatmap rescales to the selected field and emphasizes faint values. Coordinates use geometric units (G = c = 1) and an arbitrary length unit ℓ. Scaling a model to a different physical size changes its required density. Moving bubbles use comoving coordinates, so photon motion on screen is relative to the bubble.

These geometries are mathematical experiments. A viable drive would need a realizable matter source and a way to create, control, and sustain the geometry.

Numerical checks

Directional null energy

For the static shell and flat control, sample null directions relative to the radial axis. Radius is measured in simulation units.

Physical scale

Rescales the same dimensionless geometry. These are gravitational benchmarks at fixed compactness.

Graded-index optics

Compare the static matter shell's equivalent radial refractive index with a uniform medium. Predict how the wall gradient will bend an off-axis beam.

The analog reproduces spatial light paths for the static shell. It uses a material index profile and models no change to the surrounding spacetime.
